Shown while servers are connected: Android needs it to let players reach them from the background.
Each server shows up in the system\'s file picker: any app can open its files from there.
Reach an NFSv4.2 export on the local network (TCP) or over the VPN through the gateway (QUIC).
Servers connect by themselves when an app opens one of their files.
%1$d/%2$d connections up · %3$d in flight · reading %4$d files
No answer (%1$s): tried again when the network changes
What you changed on this server is not saved.
It disappears from the file pickers. Nothing on the server is deleted.
Where the server is and how to reach it
As it shows in the file pickers
Straight to nfsd. For the local network: no loss there, so it is as fast and uses less battery.
Through the gateway next to nfsd. For the VPN and networks with loss: many streams in one connection, and it recovers at once when the network changes.
nfsd\'s name or address, and its TCP port (2049).
The gateway\'s name and its UDP port (443 unless NFS_GATEWAY_LISTEN says otherwise). Nothing about nfsd: the gateway knows where it is.
Its path as the server exports it, as in a mount: / for the root.
What the export asks for (xprtsec in /etc/exports)
Nothing encrypted between the phone and nfsd: only for a network you trust.
The tunnel to the gateway is encrypted anyway; nfsd sees no TLS.
Encrypted, and nfsd\'s certificate is checked against the server\'s name.
As TLS, and the phone proves who it is with its certificate (xprtsec=mtls).
From Android\'s key store: install the .p12 in Settings › Security. The key never leaves it.
The gateway always asks for one; with mTLS, nfsd too. From Android\'s key store: the key never leaves it.
Who you are to the server\'s permissions
Your user and group on the server (id -u, id -g there). With all_squash in the export, the server ignores them.
Standard: you write, others read (files 644, folders 755). Group: your group writes too (664, 775), for shared folders. Private: only you (600, 700). Other: any mask, such as 027 (640, 750).
Group numbers that also give you access, separated by commas.
Edge cases, off by default: turn one on only if you need it
Symbolic links to their own folder or one above it open as folders. Apps that go through whole folders (copying, deleting, galleries indexing) loop through them up to 40 levels deep.
Copies within this server are made by the server: instant on XFS or btrfs, nothing through the network, but with no progress. Off, the file manager copies through the phone, with progress.
Longer: opening something again does not wait to reconnect. Shorter: less battery, and the notification goes sooner. Never: connected until the server is turned off.

Proxy: every write goes to the server through Android\'s file proxy, which adds a cost to each one: slow when apps write in small pieces, but the app knows when the server has it all. Local copy: the app writes a real file on the phone at full speed, uploaded as it grows; it may finish before the upload does (its progress and any error show in a notification). Edited files always use the proxy.
This server\'s lines in nfs-log.txt (Android/data/<app>/files; Activity shares it). Network and service lines are always kept.
Only what failed: could not connect, an operation or an upload failed, the link test failed.
Errors, and what went slow or could not be done: thumbnails over 2 s or not made.
Warnings, and what helps compare: each connection, each upload with its figures, the link test.
Everything: also each file opened (mode and way), each thumbnail made and each idle disconnection.

Categories. connection: connected (transport and security), could not connect, closed when unused. files: operations that failed (list, open, read, write, create, rename, delete, copy, move, with the path and the error) and each file opened. uploads: size, time, speed, way (proxy, local copy or why the proxy), and where the time went: writing (the app had it open), core (waiting on the network or the server) and closing (after the app closed it); failed uploads. thumbnails: time, bytes and reads, or why it could not be made. test: the link test\'s result.
How many are used at once; 0 picks for the transport (%d). With loss, more of them fill the link better; the server needs threads for them.
How far ahead of a player it reads, from 16 MB to 1 GB: the first 48 MB in memory, the rest in the local cache.
Keeps what was read on the phone: seeing it again needs no network.
Off, it disappears from the file pickers and never connects; its settings stay.
Apps cannot create, change or delete files on this server.
Connects with the settings above, before saving them
Connected in %1$d ms · %2$d entries at the root · %3$s free of %4$s
no answer in %d s: check the address, the port and the transport
No server connected. They connect when an app opens one of their files, or when you test one.
The last part of nfs-log.txt: connections, network changes and errors. It holds your servers\' names.
Throughput and connections while servers are connected; Android requires it
For every server; Android may empty it when it runs short of space
0 turns it off. It never leaves less than 1 GB free, and a new size applies to connections made after.
What was read will come from the network again.
Through which network it is reached
Tried on any network. With nobody answering it fails in 4 s, and is not tried again until the network changes.
Only while a network of this kind gives the phone an address in this subnet (which VPN, which Wi-Fi); empty for any. Without it, the server fails at once instead of waiting.
An address and its prefix, as 198.51.100.0/24
